This is a list of the world's countries and their dependencies by land, water, and total area, ranked by total area.


Entries in this list include, but are not limited to, those in the ISO 3166-1 standard, which includes sovereign states and dependent territories. All 193 member states of the United Nations plus the two observer states are given a rank number. Largely unrecognised states not in ISO 3166-1 are included in the list in ranked order. </fragment>

</fragment>

7. **^**  Largest English-speaking country by land area and largest country in the Western Hemisphere by land area (second-largest by total area after Canada). Figures for total area and water area include all coastal and territorial waters.

article_title: List of countries by life expectancy

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>

</fragment>

10. **^** "Life expectancy and Healthy life expectancy, data by WHO region". World Health Organization. 7 December 2022.
11. **^** "The World Factbook — Central Intelligence Agency". *www.cia.gov*.
12. **^** "Life expectancy at birth - The World Factbook". *www.cia.gov*. Retrieved 27 July 2022.

## External links

[edit]

* Global Agewatch Archived 3 October 2014 at the Wayback Machine has the latest internationally comparable statistics on life expectancy from 195 countries.
* Life expectancy trends interactive graph

</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

article_title: List of countries by life expectancy

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]

[edit]

</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.

<title>Health in the United States</title>
<fragment>

![](image)Historical development of life expectancy
Health may refer to "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease and infirmity.", according to the World Health Organization (WHO).[1] 78.7 was the average life expectancy for individuals at birth in 2017.[2] The highest cause of death for United States citizens is heart disease.[2] Infectious diseases such as sexually transmitted diseases impact the health of approximately 19 million yearly.[3] The two most commonly reported infectious diseases include chlamydia and gonorrhea. The United States is currently challenged by the COVID-19 pandemic, and is 19th in the world in COVID-19 vaccination rates.[4] All 50 states in the U.S. require immunizations for children in order to enroll in public school, but various exemptions are available by state. Immunizations are often compulsory for military enlistment in the United States.[5]

Starting 2000, there was significant growth in spending for public healthcare[33] and in 2006 it exceed the pre-1991 level in real terms.[33] Also life expectancy increased from 1991–93 levels, infant mortality rate dropped from 18.1 in 1995 to 8.4 in 2008.[34]


In May 2012 Putin signed the May Decrees which included a plan to double the wages of healthcare staff by 2018 and gradual privatisation of state health services. In November 2014 the wage rises in Moscow led to the closure of 15 hospitals and 7,000 redundancies.[2]


In 2011, Moscow's government launched a major project known as UMIAS as part of its electronic healthcare initiative. UMIAS stands for Integrated Medical Information and Analytical System of Moscow.[35] The aim of the project is to make healthcare more convenient and accessible for Muscovites.

Based on my research from Wikipedia articles and health data sources, I can provide you with a comparative analysis of healthcare systems, life expectancy, and COVID-19 impacts across Russia, Canada, China, the United States, and Brazil.

## Healthcare System Overview

**Canada:** Operates a universal healthcare system where healthcare is publicly funded and available to all citizens. The Commonwealth Fund report ranked Canada slightly above average in life expectancy among developed nations.

**United States:** Has a mixed public-private system with the highest healthcare spending among developed countries ($10,447 average in 2018), yet ranks below other developed nations in life expectancy outcomes.

**Brazil:** Healthcare is a constitutional right provided through the Unified Health System (SUS), which is universal and free for everyone - both Brazilian permanent residents and foreigners. It's a mix of private and government institutions.

**Russia:** Has experienced significant reforms since 2000, with healthcare spending growing and exceeding pre-1991 levels by 2006 in real terms. Life expectancy improved from the 1991-93 low points after Soviet collapse.

**China:** Has shown dramatic health improvements since 1949, with life expectancy increasing from 41.6 years in 1950 to approximately 77 years in 2011.

## Life Expectancy Data

**Pre-COVID Era:**
- **Canada:** Women have life expectancy of 84.1 years, with women at 65 having 22.2 more years (87.5 total), men at 65 having 19.5 more years (84.5 total)
- **Brazil:** Life expectancy reached 76.6 years in 2019
- **United States:** Average life expectancy was 78.7 years in 2017, but ranked toward the bottom among developed nations at 78.6 years according to Commonwealth Fund
- **China:** Life expectancy reached 75.0 years by 2011 (likely higher now)
- **Russia:** Life expectancy increased significantly from post-Soviet decline but still lower than other large nations

## COVID-19 Impact

**United States:** Experienced the most dramatic life expectancy decline. Life expectancy "plunged in 2020, especially for Black and Hispanic Americans" and "continued to fall in 2021 as COVID, drug deaths surged." Multiple sources confirm this was the most significant decline among developed nations.

**Other Nations:** While specific 2021 COVID impact data for Russia, Canada, China, and Brazil wasn't detailed in the sources found, all nations experienced pandemic impacts to varying degrees. The United States data suggests it was particularly hard hit in terms of life expectancy reduction.

## Key Health Indicators

**Brazil (2019):**
- Infant mortality rate: 10 deaths per 1000 live births
- Total fertility rate: 1.6 births per woman

**China (2017):**
- Infant mortality rate: 10 deaths per 1000 live births  
- Total fertility rate: 1.6 children per woman

**Canada:**
- Under-five mortality rate decreased from 20.9 per 1000 (1971) to 4.98 per 1000 (2020)

**Russia:**
- Infant mortality rate dropped from 18.1 in 1995 to 8.4 in 2008
- Significant improvements in healthcare spending and outcomes since 2000

## Comparative Summary

The United States demonstrates the paradox of highest healthcare spending with relatively poorer health outcomes compared to other developed nations, a situation worsened by COVID-19. Canada's universal system delivers above-average outcomes, while Brazil's constitutional right to healthcare provides universal access despite being a developing economy. China shows remarkable progress from very low post-WWII levels, and Russia has recovered significantly from post-Soviet health crises.

All these nations faced COVID-19 challenges, but the United States appears to have suffered the most severe life expectancy decline according to the available sources.

- **Canada** increased from 39.0 years in 1831 to 83.7 years in 2015-2020
- **China** increased from 43.8 years in 1950-1955 to 75.7 years in 2010-2015

The recent declines in US and Russian life expectancy are notable, particularly Russia's significant drop from 73.34 to 70.06 years between 2019 and 2021.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.

<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>List of countries by life expectancy</title>
<fragment>
The life expectancy is shown separately for males and for females, as well as a combined figure. Several non-sovereign entities and territories are also included in this list.


The figures reflect the quality of healthcare in the countries listed as well as other factors including HIV infections.


From the beginning of the current century there is a tendency to also estimate **Healthy life expectancy** (HALE) — the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health".[1][2]


Comparing life expectancies across countries can be problematic. For example, due to poor reporting in some countries and various local standards in collecting statistics. This is especially true for Healthy life expectancy, the definition of which criteria may change over time, even within a country.



## World Bank Group (2021)

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.




## Methodology

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

![](image)
![](image)
![](image)
Life expectancy in world, according to estimation of the World Bank Group, 2019–2021

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.

## United Nations (2021)

[edit]

Shown is the "period life expectancy" at birth. This is the average number of years a newborn would live if age-specific mortality rates in the current year were to stay the same throughout its life. The data is taken from the 2020 and 2022 United Nations World Population Prospects.[6][7] It is also used to calculate the Human Development Index. Only countries with populations over 50,000 are listed. Due to this criterion, the table does not include Monaco (LE 85.9 years, population 39,000). By default, the list is sorted by 2021. Data for 2021 can also be viewed via Our World in Data.[8]

Based on the Wikipedia data I found, here are the key demographic differences between Japan, Canada, and Nigeria:

## **Age Structure**

**Japan (Aged Population):**
- 0-14 years: 11.98%
- 15-64 years: 59.32%
- 65+ years: 28.70%

**Canada (Aging Population):**
- 0-14 years: 16.61%
- 15-64 years: 66.50%
- 65+ years: 16.89%

**Nigeria (Youthful Population):**
- 0-14 years: 42.67%
- 15-64 years: 54.58%
- 65+ years: 2.75%

## **Life Expectancy**

**Japan (Highest):**
- 2015-2020: 84.4 years (world's highest)
- Has remarkably high life expectancy, especially for women

**Canada (High):**
- 1985-1990: 76.8 years
- Consistently high, but lower than Japan

**Nigeria (Lowest):**
- 2022: 61.33 years (Male: 59.51, Female: 63.27)
- Significantly lower than developed nations

## **Fertility Rates**

**Japan (Very Low):**
- 2022: 1.26 (among world's lowest, far below replacement rate of 2.1)
- Facing severe population decline concerns

**Canada (Low):**
- Below replacement rate, but higher than Japan

**Nigeria (Very High):**
- 2022: 4.62 children per woman
- One of the world's highest fertility rates

## **Population Dynamics**

**Japan:** 
- Rapidly aging society with declining birth rates
- Government calling it a "now or never" crisis

**Canada:**
- Moderate growth supported by immigration (projected 400,000+ annually)
- Gradually aging but more balanced than Japan

**Nigeria:**
- Explosive young population growth
- Urbanizing rapidly (53.5% urban population)
- High population growth rate

## **Key Contrasts**

1. **Japan**: Demographic crisis with aging population and declining births
2. **Canada**: Managed aging with immigration support
3. **Nigeria**: Youth bulge with high fertility and rapid urbanization

These three countries represent three completely different demographic challenges and opportunities in today's world.

<fragment>
 
This **list of countries by life expectancy** provides a comprehensive list of countries alongside their respective life expectancy figures. The data is differentiated by gender, presenting life expectancies for males, females, and a combined average. In addition to sovereign nations, the list encompasses several non-sovereign entities and territories. The figures serve as an indicator of the quality of healthcare in the respective countries and are influenced by various factors, including the prevalence of diseases such as HIV/AIDS. This article introduces the concept of Healthy life expectancy (HALE), which denotes the average number of years a person is expected to live in "full health". There are challenges in comparing life expectancies across countries due to disparities in data reporting and collection standards. The primary source of the most recent data presented is the World Bank Group's 2021 report.
